routes.description: Establish historical credibility for bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity through early Pauline testimony, substantively stable textual transmission, external identification of early Christian belief, and persistence of apostolic church structures and doctrines.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Paul warrants a bodily-resurrection reading, transmission and hostile-witness evidence reliably identify early Christian belief, and institutional and doctrinal continuities connect the first-century church with later Catholic and related apostolic communions.

motionBridge.description: Connect the Pauline, transmission, hostile-witness, and church-structure evidence to the historical credibility of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the early undisputed Pauline letters attest a real bodily resurrection and a risen-Christ appearance rather than merely an immaterial vision.
Establish that manuscript stability and external testimony preserve and independently identify an early, historically rooted Christian belief tradition.
Trace first-century leadership offices and essential doctrines through the pre-Nicene period and later apostolic communions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Roman, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac differences coexist with substantial agreement on essential doctrines, councils, and apostolic orders.
Distinguish reforms that retained inherited Catholic doctrine from later movements that discarded it when characterizing historical continuity.

routes.description: Deny that the cited materials establish bodily resurrection or a uniquely Catholic lineage by emphasizing visionary and secondhand alternatives for Paul, uncertainty in transmission and preservation, early Christian diversity, and context-dependent religious branching.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline reports remain compatible with visionary or inherited interpretations, surviving sources cannot securely overcome transmission and selection uncertainty, or early diversity and later branching prevent identification of one continuous Catholic institution.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence named in the motion remains insufficient to make bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity historically credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and witness traditions do not establish a bodily encounter or independently prove an earlier resurrection event.
Show that copying gaps, oral and written transmission, authorial selection, and selective survival limit the evidential force of Christian and hostile sources.
Show that competing early groups, divergent regional churches, and conciliar formation complicate identification of a uniquely continuous Catholic orthodoxy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the continuity case to distinguish the existence of a small pre-Constantinian group from widespread or uniquely authoritative orthodoxy.
Use earlier reform movements and shared Christian scripture and history to test claims that later divisions constitute categorical religious rupture.

sections.title: Pauline evidence and bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: The earliest Pauline material is central to whether the resurrection claim concerns a tangible risen body and whether Paul's reported experience and inherited witness list provide independent historical support.

sections.title: Textual stability and Gospel transmission
sections.rationale: Historical use of Christian writings depends on distinguishing substantive manuscript stability from uncertainty about earlier sources, interpolations, transmission across decades, and authorial selection.

sections.title: Hostile witnesses and preservation effects
sections.rationale: External descriptions may help identify early Christian beliefs, but their force depends on whether surviving hostile materials independently represent the period or reflect selective preservation.

sections.title: Early orthodoxy and institutional continuity
sections.rationale: The Catholic-continuity burden turns on whether first-century leadership structures persist through the pre-Nicene era despite a small population, competing groups, councils, and uncertainty about early development.

sections.title: Apostolic communions, reform, and religious branching
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, and Protestant traditions test whether shared doctrine, councils, orders, scripture, and history demonstrate continuity or instead support multiple context-dependent Christian branches.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Paul's early undisputed letters attest that he believed Christ underwent bodily resurrection and that Paul experienced an appearance of the risen Christ.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies himself as Catholic and advances the affirmative historical case associated with William Albrecht.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly introduces the affirmative Pauline premise, so no earlier opposing move is available or required for response contact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the central Pauline claim but supplies only a compressed textual bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and confines itself to early Pauline letters while acknowledging that their details are not fully developed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges limited detail, but the excerpt does not itself demonstrate both bodily resurrection and the character of Paul's appearance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but the bridge from an early belief in resurrection to a bodily appearance experienced by Paul remains material and compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The early Pauline corpus is identified, but no specific passage or analysis within the excerpt establishes both elements of the proposition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable Pauline bodily-resurrection bridge and sits near the top of the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its own textual thesis without materially developing or evaluating a live rival interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly restricts the case to early Pauline letters, concedes sparse detail, and claims they still show bodily resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Paul's early letters do not establish a bodily encounter because his experience may have been visionary and cannot by itself prove an alleged resurrection years earlier.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker rejects the affirmative reading of Paul and articulates the skeptical historical position associated with Graham Oppy.

components.text: Whether the early Pauline material establishes a bodily risen-Christ encounter rather than merely reporting resurrection belief.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies that the letters support a meeting of two bodies and distinguishes a possible vision from proof of an earlier resurrection event.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive bodily-encounter inference and states the resulting limitation on historical proof.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between a bodily meeting, a vision, and proof of an earlier event is clear and consistently scoped to Paul's letters.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply advances a possibility and an evidential limitation rather than claiming to disprove resurrection, matching the support presented.

charity.alternative: Paul believed Christ was bodily raised even if the appearance account lacks sensory detail.
charity.decisiveQualification: Belief in bodily resurrection does not by itself establish that Paul's own encounter was bodily or independently prove the earlier event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between visionary content and independent proof is clear, consistent, and leaves only a bounded implicit account of the textual evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evidential caution is well framed, but the excerpt asserts what the early letters lack without representative textual comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge by challenging both bodily encounter and independent proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the distinction between Pauline belief and the stronger historical inference, though it does not analyze particular passages.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that the early letters do not support a bodily meeting and that a vision cannot itself prove an event years earlier.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: The contrast between mortal and spiritual bodies in 1 Corinthians 15 is best understood as describing a tangible, real, physical resurrected body rather than an immaterial body.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker describes his own Greek study, identifies himself as Catholic, and defends Albrecht's affirmative Pauline interpretation.

components.text: Whether Paul's language supports a tangible resurrected body despite the proposed visionary interpretation of his experience.

response.rationale: The reply addresses the bodily-versus-immaterial issue through 1 Corinthians 15, but it does not independently answer the objection that Paul's appearance may have been visionary.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive bodily-language component but leaves the distinct character and evidential status of Paul's encounter unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but tangible, real, physical, and spiritual body are asserted as aligned without a clarifying semantic account.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying there is no other way to read the passage substantially exceeds the excerpt's undeveloped comparison with an immaterial reading.

charity.alternative: A spiritual body in 1 Corinthians 15 may be transformed or nonordinary without being straightforwardly physical.
charity.decisiveQualification: The rival reading requires lexical and contextual comparison rather than dismissal merely because the speaker favors tangibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific Pauline chapter and contrast are identified, but no language, context, or rival exegesis is supplied to warrant exclusivity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge on the meaning of the resurrected body.

representationalCharity.rationale: The alternative is mentioned through Dan Barker, but it is dismissed without presenting its strongest textual basis or decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites the mortal-versus-spiritual-body contrast in 1 Corinthians 15 and asserts that the spiritual body is tangible and physical.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy

moves.attributionBasis: The speaker presses the skeptical dating and source-selection challenge characteristic of Graham Oppy's position throughout the exchange.

precisionFindings.rationale: The identification thesis is recoverable, but hostile, early, scriptural markers, and the relevant Christian group are insufficiently delimited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Generic pagan descriptions and belief markers are invoked without naming representative sources or demonstrating independence and coverage.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges competing groups but compresses the strongest selection and identification qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says pagan opponents describe worship of Christ as God and claims their identity markers correspond to scripture rather than Gnosticism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The first centuries contained many competing Christian groups, so identifying one properly orthodox lineage before councils fixed orthodoxy is historically unwarranted.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly qualifies his expertise while giving Oppy's skeptical account of early diversity and conciliar definition.

components.text: Whether hostile descriptions justify identifying one early scriptural and orthodox Christian group amid competing groups.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the identification of a settled orthodoxy by emphasizing numerous competing groups before councils defined doctrinal boundaries.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive single-orthodoxy inference, though it does not separately analyze the hostile sources themselves.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal scope and council-based thesis are clear, but Orthodox and nailed down compress distinctions between emerging norms and formal definition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker qualifies his knowledge, but the claim that nothing was orthodox before councils is stronger than the cited diversity alone warrants.

charity.alternative: A recognizable proto-orthodox lineage could exist before councils formally codified its doctrines.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior existence would not by itself show unique authority or settled boundaries amid multiple competing groups.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Diversity and later conciliar definition support caution, but the inference that no orthodoxy existed beforehand is materially stronger than the premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on a broad historical characterization and explicit uncertainty without representative groups, dates, or conciliar developments.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central diversity-against-single-lineage bridge by challenging preconciliar identification.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possibility is responsibly framed, but the excerpt provides no concrete preservation pattern or omitted hostile source.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central transmission-selection uncertainty bridge as applied to hostile-source survival.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection does not allege tampering and accurately limits itself to representativeness, preserving the strongest benign alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly presents selection as a possible hypothesis affecting pagan evidence for widespread orthodoxy before councils.

moves.proposition: Christianity was relatively small and not widespread before Constantine, in part because it had not yet been legalized.
